judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's recomputations are correct where it made them: ranges 0, 22, 0, 2, 0, 5; Class A mean 32, range 45, median 30, Q1 20, Q3 40, IQR 20; Class B range 12 and IQR 5; the difference 33; and P(more than 30) = 4/10 = 2/5. The dot plots do agree with the listed data. But the judge scored mathematical_correctness and answer_key_quality 4 without testing the one claim on the sheet that is false. Problem 6 plants Sam's median of 35 from the unsorted list 30, 45, 20, 15, 60, 30, 25, 40, 20, 35, and the key states "Sam took the middle of the list as written rather than of the sorted values, and landed on 35". Take the middle of that list as written and you get the 5th and 6th entries, 60 and 30, averaging 45 — not 35, which is simply the last value typed. The Common wrong answers block prints the same false causal claim as grading guidance. It survived because verify.json declares the trap as {"expr": "35", "value": 35}: a bare literal, so check_traps only proved 35 != 30. Separately, problem 8 prints answer slots for Class B's Q1 and Q3 that no verify entry covers, and Class B's mean of 33 is asserted in problem 10's stem with no stats entry behind it.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 1 and 2 are the best teaching move on the sheet and should be preserved exactly: the same question with one word changed ("How tall is Priya?" against "How tall are the students in our class?"), each with its own dot plot, so "statistical" gets an operational definition — range 0 against range 22 — instead of a vocabulary rule.

Problem 7's key justifies the IQR rather than defining it: delete the 60-minute student and the range collapses from 45 to 30 while the IQR does not move at all, "because the middle five values are untouched".

The quartile convention is stated in the directions block ("split them into a lower half and an upper half, and take the median of each half") before any problem uses it, so the student is not left guessing which of the competing school methods this sheet means.
Problem 9's key surfaces the subtlety instead of hiding it: two students land exactly on the median, so "more than 30" gives 4/10 and not 1/2 — a detail most sheets round away.

root_causes.description: validate_traps accepts any numeric string as a trap expr, including a bare constant. check_traps then proves only that the constant differs from the expected answer, never that the named misconception applied to the problem's givens produces it — so a false causal claim can be printed as machine-backed grading guidance.
evidence: verify.json id 6 trap: {"desc": "took the middle value of the unsorted list instead of sorting first", "expr": "35", "value": 35}.
The worksheet's printed unsorted list is 30, 45, 20, 15, 60, 30, 25, 40, 20, 35; its 5th and 6th entries are 60 and 30, so the named method yields 45. 35 is the last entry, not the middle.
answer_key.pdf problem 6: "Sam took the middle of the list as written rather than of the sorted values, and landed on 35."
scripts/verify.py check_traps concedes in its own docstring that "desc-to-expr correspondence stays the author's claim"; the guard at lines 960-975 only compares values.

root_causes.description: Verification is declared per problem id rather than per printed answer slot, so a multi-blank stem can carry fewer verify entries than it has blanks and still report full coverage.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 8 prints "Class B: Q1 = ___ Q3 = ___ IQR = ___"; verify.json id 8 declares range, iqr and a read_data difference only, so Q1 and Q3 are unverified (the key's 30 and 35 are in fact correct).
worksheet.pdf problem 10's stem asserts "Class B's mean is 33 minutes" with no stats entry for it anywhere in verify.json.
The machine observation records unique_verified_problems 10 of 10 and problem_count_matches true, so nothing signals the gap.

root_causes.description: Six problems demand written answers and only problem 10 is declared manual, so the sheet's many short-explanation slots are delivered unrecorded.
evidence: Unflagged written demands: problem 1 "So is 'How tall is Priya?' a statistical question?"; problem 2 "What single word made the difference?"; problem 3 "Write the rule you used in your own words" plus a four-row statistical? tick column; problem 5 "what does that range tell a teacher that the mean does not?"; problem 6 "What exactly did Sam do wrong?"; problem 8 "Which class is easier to predict, and why?".
verify.json holds exactly one manual entry, on problem 10.

improvements.title: Reject a bare numeric literal as a misconception trap's expr
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/verify.py validate_traps, reject a trap whose expr parses to a plain number with no operator and no symbol bound from the problem's givens: the wrong-method ARITHMETIC has to be written out ((60+30)/2, 5/7, 8*x*y) so check_traps can prove the misconception really produces the printed number. Emit a teaching message saying so. For data-driven types (stats, read_data, probability), allow the trap to name the wrong measure or the wrong data subset instead of an expression, and compute it, so the same guarantee extends to sheets whose givens are a list rather than an at-binding.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture reproducing this case: a stats/median problem over [15,20,20,25,30,30,35,40,45,60] whose trap is {"desc": "took the middle value of the unsorted list", "expr": "35", "value": 35}. verify.py must exit non-zero with a message demanding the arithmetic; rewriting the expr as "(60+30)/2" must then fail the value check (45 != 35), exposing the real inconsistency. Today the original fixture passes silently.
improvements.expected_impact: A declared trap stops being an unchecked authorial claim. The Common wrong answers block is printed for graders as machine-backed diagnosis, so this is the difference between a diagnostic tool and a plausible-sounding guess; two cases in this batch (curr-196 problem 6, curr-199 problem 6) use bare literals and one of them is wrong.
improvements.risk: Some legitimate traps are genuinely a constant a student writes from misreading a figure or an axis label; those need the data-driven escape hatch, or authors will be pushed into inventing arithmetic that did not happen.

improvements.title: Require one verify entry per printed answer slot, not per problem id
improvements.proposed_change: Extend tests/check_answer_line.py to count the response slots inside each \problem block (\ansblank, \answerline, and the inline "X = ___" runs these sheets use) and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying an expected for that id, naming the uncovered slot. SKILL.md should state the rule as "every blank the student fills is either machine-verified or declared manual".
improvements.regression_test: New fixture: a stem printing "Q1 = ___ Q3 = ___ IQR = ___" beside a verify.json declaring only the iqr entry for that id. check_answer_line.py must exit non-zero naming two uncovered slots; adding q1 and q3 entries makes it pass. Fails today — this task ships exactly that shape with every gate green.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the dominant coverage gap in the run. On this sheet it forces Q1 and Q3 for Class B into the verified set; on curr-197 the same rule would have caught a printed median that is actually wrong.
improvements.risk: Slot counting from LaTeX is approximate — a stem that lays out a worked table or a units label could be miscounted — so the counter must bind to the shipped answer macros rather than to loose underscores, and authors need a way to declare an intentionally unfilled prompt line.

improvements.title: Fail the build when a problem stem asks for reasoning and its verify entry is machine-only
improvements.proposed_change: Add a delivery-blocking lint that pairs the worksheet source with the verify JSON: scan each \problem block for an open-response demand ("explain", "say why", "say how you decided", "in one sentence", "what went wrong", "find her mistake", "describe", "sketch", "plot", "graph it") and fail the build when that problem id carries no {"type": "manual"} entry. SKILL.md should state the rule positively: a problem that asks for a value AND a sentence gets TWO verify entries, the machine one for the value and a manual one carrying the full-credit criteria, exactly as this run already does elsewhere.
improvements.regression_test: New fixture pair under tests/fixtures: a worksheet .tex whose problem 3 stem ends "Explain in one sentence why ..." beside a verify.json whose id 3 holds only an eval entry. tests/check_prose_consistency.py must exit non-zero naming problem 3; adding {"id": 3, "type": "manual", "desc": ...} makes it exit 0. The test fails today because no checker reads the stem for open-response prose.
improvements.expected_impact: The gate chain's manual-flag count starts telling the truth, so a grader is told which written answers nobody machine-checked instead of reading "nothing is flagged for manual review" under a sheet full of explanation prompts. On curr-196 the manual count moves from 1 to roughly 7, which matches a sheet whose central skill — deciding whether a question is statistical and saying why — is answered in words.
improvements.risk: Keyword matching will flag stems whose imperative is decorative ("show your work"), so the lint needs a curated phrase list and an explicit per-problem opt-out, or authors will start declaring hollow manual entries to silence it.

case_summary: A well-built concept sheet: the one-word change between problems 1 and 2 gives "statistical question" an operational definition, the Class A / Class B comparison makes centre-without-spread concretely misleading, and the key argues for the IQR by deleting the outlier and showing what moves. Every centre, spread, quartile and probability I recomputed is right. But problem 6's planted misconception is false as printed: taking the middle of the unsorted list 30, 45, 20, 15, 60, 30, 25, 40, 20, 35 gives 45, not the 35 the key attributes to it, and the Common wrong answers block passes that false causal claim to the grader. It survived because the trap's expr is the bare literal "35", which check_traps can only compare against the answer. Problem 8 also prints Class B Q1 and Q3 slots that no entry covers, problem 10's stem asserts an unverified Class B mean of 33, and six problems ask for written answers with only problem 10 declared manual.
